text: The back of a police van is maybe eight square metres, and the people locked into it would cross the street to avoid each other. Cairo, summer 2013, the weeks after Morsi was pushed out: detainees from opposite sides of that argument, and from different streets and classes, loaded into the same box by the same men. The setting is also the constraint. A film held inside a truck cannot cut away to explain the city, so the unrest outside arrives as noise, as heat, as shapes through the mesh, and every disagreement is conducted at arm's length by people who cannot walk away. Ninety-five minutes is brisk for a thriller and very long for a confinement. Egypt sent it to the Academy Awards, willing to look at that week from inside the vehicle.

A policeman on leave keeps to his professional habits: he watches a local man, logs his movements, assembles a case — and the case concerns his own dead wife. She was killed on a road, in an accident, and what he suspects is that she had been unfaithful before the road took her. Hlynur Pálmason sets this in a remote Icelandic town, which limits the number of people a suspicion can be spread across; the suspect is somebody the chief will meet at the shop, at the school gate, on the one road out. Grief here is not a mood but a workload, pursued with the only competence the man has. The performance took the European Film Award for best actor, and the demand behind that is plain in the setup: hold sympathy for a man turning himself into a surveillance operation.

The prescription arrives on cassette tape: one task a day, to be completed and then photographed with a Polaroid, the photograph kept as proof. A sweeping amnesia has emptied people of their histories, and the medical answer to it is administrative — a programme that issues a new life in instalments, at the pace of a man who cannot remember the old one. The listing says comedy as well as drama, and the premise only holds if it is played flat, with the doctors entirely sincere. Nothing in the treatment is digital. A biography rebuilt from tape and instant film is made of objects: countable, misplaceable, thin enough to carry in a coat pocket. Ninety-one minutes. The European University Film Award, voted by students, went to Christos Nikou's film, which suits a story about being told what to do next.

One soldier steps between three others and a Muslim civilian, and the film treats that minute as the opening of an account rather than the end of a story. Bosnia, 1993; the intervention costs him gravely, and Srdan Golubović sets nearly everything else twelve years later, among the people that minute implicated, in a society small enough that they can all still find each other. The case is a real one. That matters less as a guarantee of accuracy than as a limit: an actual event cannot be tidied by a screenwriter, and gratitude, guilt and grievance do not settle at the same rate. A hundred minutes, only a few of them at the war. Sundance gave it a special jury prize; the film's own subject is what does not travel, a debt that stays in the neighbourhood where it was incurred.

A civil war starts, the school closes, and for two teenagers that is at first the best news of the year. Beirut, 1975. Tarek and Omar have a city suddenly short of adult supervision, and the film is billed as comedy and romance as much as drama, which fits the way catastrophe first registers on the young: as holiday, then as inconvenience, then as a line that cannot be crossed. The line is literal here. It separates west from east, Muslim from Christian, and the boys' decision to go over it turns an errand into something their parents cannot undo. The war stays mostly at the edges of what they can see, which is about as much of it as they can afford to notice. Ziad Doueiri made this in 1998 and set it in the first months, before anyone inside the story knows the scale of what has begun.

An Arab surgeon in Tel Aviv has built a life on being the exception, and an exception holds only as long as nothing happens. Then a suicide bombing tears through the city and the wounded arrive where he works. What follows is not a procedural. The pressure comes from a discovery about the person he knows best, and from the fact that a man in his position cannot ask questions privately: every inquiry is made as an Arab, in front of colleagues, police and neighbours who liked him yesterday. Ziad Doueiri directs, on Belgian money, in English, across a border most productions decline to cross. A hundred and two minutes, largely conversation, all of it conducted by someone with markedly less standing than he had that morning.

Summits happen in hotels, which makes a political thriller set at one a film about corridors, adjoining suites, and who is seen leaving whose door. Santiago Mitre installs an Argentine president, Hernán Blanco, in exactly that architecture: a meeting of Latin American heads of state in Chile, where regional alliances are being rearranged and every conversation has a second audience. Family trouble follows him in. What would elsewhere be ordinary private difficulty becomes, in this company, material — the sort of thing other delegations can price. The film runs 114 minutes and spends much of that on waiting, which is most of what negotiation consists of. Blanco is watched at rest more than in office, and rest is where the questions about him accumulate.

A fifty-two-year-old woman rents an apartment for herself, and everyone she is related to treats it as an emergency. Manana has been living with three generations in one Georgian house: parents, husband, grown children, their partners, all fluent in her business. Her family's first demand is a cause — something nameable, something that can be argued with or repaired. The film is under no obligation to hand them one, and its patience lies in watching the demand repeat itself in kitchens, at the door, down the phone, by people convinced they are helping. A hundred and nineteen minutes in Georgian, most of it talk aimed at a woman rather than to her. Whatever she finds in the new flat has to compete with all that noise; the wager is that quiet can.

A woman whose husband is missing is not a widow, and the difference is administrative as much as private. Fahrije's husband has not come back from the war in Kosovo. Nothing has been declared, so nothing can be settled, and in the meantime there are children to feed. She starts a small business, which in her village means seeking permission from people who were never asked their opinion of her and intend to give it anyway. Blerta Basholli keeps the obstacles unglamorous: a signature, a rumour, a road, one remark repeated by enough neighbours that it acquires the force of law. Eighty-four minutes, tightly kept. The Sundance audience gave it their award, an odd reception for a film whose central action is a woman deciding to earn money while her husband's status stays open.

Refuse collection is night work, and night work hands a man the run of a city that believes itself empty. Sergio rides the truck through Lisbon in the small hours, handling what other people have finished with, then keeps going after the shift for encounters he does not name and does not repeat. João Pedro Rodrigues films this without the consolations usually granted such a character: no confidant, little speech, no interior monologue to translate what he wants into something discussable. Desire runs closer to scent and pursuit than to romance, and the attention paid to bodies is the same attention paid to the machinery of the job. Eighty-seven minutes, released in 2000, still not a comfortable object — the discomfort structural rather than shocking, a matter of being kept beside a man who will not explain himself.

A man goes into a river valley in northern Portugal to count birds, and the valley declines to stay scenery. The premise is deliberately thin: an ornithologist stranded, then put through a sequence of trials arranged like the Stations of the Cross, brutal in places and erotic in others, with no assurance that the two will stay apart. João Pedro Rodrigues keeps the birdwatcher's register — patience, distance, the discipline of not intervening — and lets it drift toward hagiography, which is also a form built on one man being tested alone. A hundred and eighteen minutes, most of them spent with a single body in a landscape. What sustains it is the reversal in the looking: the specialist observer becomes the observed, tracked through country whose other inhabitants have their own plans for him.

Two villages within sight of one another, and three love stories set in three consecutive decades — the same impossibility, attempted again under changed conditions. Dalibor Matanić's structure is the argument: enmity between these neighbours is not an event with a beginning and an end but a climate that re-forms around whoever happens to be young. Each decade hands its couple a different version of the same terrain, and the later pairs inherit wreckage the earlier ones were still making. Romance is not quite the word for what any of them do; attraction works here as a measuring instrument, registering precisely what a village will tolerate this year. A hundred and twenty-three minutes. The European Film Award voted by the public went to it, which is worth noting for a film that offers audiences so little comfort.

Everything in the valley happens in front of the horses, and the film relays it that way: rural Icelandic affairs as the animals take them in. That angle carries the comedy, since courtship, rivalry and vanity look ridiculous from a paddock, and it flattens the darker turns, because an animal registers events without ranking them. Benedikt Erlingsson works in episodes across country where everyone can see everyone, so a private humiliation becomes a public one within the hour. Love and death arrive in the same weather. Eighty-five minutes, mostly outdoors, with speech kept to what people say when they know they are being watched from across the fields. The Nordic Council Film Prize went to it, which suggests the region recognised its own manners in the joke.

Driving strangers for an app is work made of small courtesies performed for people who never look at the driver. Ralphie does that by day and builds his body in his own time, and something has to fill the space between the two: a group of men who call themselves a brotherhood, organised on libertarian principles, offering what the shifts do not — a rank, a name, a story about why he feels owed. John Trengove stages the recruitment as a seduction, which is what it is, and the mystery in the billing comes from how little Ralphie will admit, to anyone, himself included. Ninety-six minutes, present day, the training regime and the doctrine tightening at the same rate. Audiences have scored it low, and the film seems built to earn that: it allows no distance from its man's appetite.
